strengths: ColorCtrl addresses a useful editing problem with a simple, training-free combination of attention-map transfer and spatially masked value-token transfer. Its application across image, video, and instruction-based models is practically appealing.

The reported improvements over training-free baselines are substantial and consistent across two image backbones and CogVideoX. On ColorCtrl-Bench with FLUX.1-dev, Canny SSIM reaches 0.9324 versus 0.8832 for the strongest baseline, while also improving editing alignment.

The appendix strengthens the evidence with additional structural and editing-quality metrics, quantitative real-image comparisons, failure cases, and a human study. Table 12 provides encouraging evidence beyond the generated-source setting.
Component ablations support the usefulness of both structure preservation and regional color preservation. Qualitative examples show compelling retention of textures, transparency, and reflections.
weaknesses: The claimed physical guarantees exceed the evidence. Transferring vision-to-vision attention does not establish that geometry, materials, illumination intensity, and light transport remain fixed. Edge similarity and background preservation cannot verify these properties, and there is no controlled rendering evaluation with known scene parameters. Most benchmark tasks concern object recoloring rather than the broader lighting claims.

The main evaluation uses backbone-generated sources with one fixed seed, rather than the original PIE-Bench images. This is useful for isolating editing but favors access to an exact source trajectory. Real-image evaluation is limited to two baselines, omits the underlying UniEdit-Flow editing pipeline and commercial models, and does not clearly identify the backbone in Table 12. No quantitative real-video evaluation is provided.

Important algorithmic details remain underspecified: whether quadrant replacement occurs before or after softmax, how normalization is handled, and how attention is aggregated and normalized for mask extraction. Replacing a post-softmax quadrant can change row sums; replacing logits does not preserve normalized attention weights. This ambiguity is especially relevant because the paper criticizes competing methods for violating attention normalization.

The human-study description is inconsistent: Appendix B.2 calls it pairwise evaluation, whereas Figure 22 presents nine alternatives and asks participants to select the best one. Table 7 reports preference shares summing to 100%, without explaining aggregation or the uncertainty estimates. Case selection is also unspecified, weakening this evidence for overall superiority.

Temporal-coherence claims are not directly evaluated: video metrics are frame-wise averages, including the additional VIEScore evaluation. Attribute re-weighting likewise lacks quantitative tests of monotonicity, localization, and preservation, or a controlled comparison with alternative weighting strategies.

The contribution is primarily an incremental refinement of existing attention-control techniques. Missing runtime, peak-memory, and cache-size measurements further limit assessment of practical significance: caching attention across layers and timesteps does not substantiate the claim of no additional computational cost. Overall, the promising empirical results are not yet sufficient to resolve the methodological and evaluation gaps.

strengths: ColorCtrl addresses a useful problem with a simple, training-free combination of attention-map replacement, regional value-token replacement, and attribute reweighting. Demonstrations span SD3, FLUX.1-dev, CogVideoX, and instruction-based editing models.

Preservation improvements are substantial and consistent across the 40-prompt PIE-Bench-derived evaluation and the 300-prompt ColorCtrl-Bench. On FLUX.1-dev, Table 1 reports Canny SSIM of 0.9196 versus 0.8639 for the strongest competing editing baseline, while also improving background preservation and CLIP alignment over the editing baselines.

The supplementary evaluation meaningfully strengthens the evidence: gradient-based metrics, VIEScore assessments, and real-input comparisons in Table 12 support improvements beyond the main synthetic-image benchmarks.

The component ablation supports the usefulness of both preservation mechanisms. Qualitative examples show convincing retention of textures, transparency, and reflections, and the paper acknowledges localization and inversion failures.
weaknesses: The physical-consistency claims exceed the evidence. Copying visual attention does not establish that geometry, material parameters, illumination intensity, and light transport remain fixed, despite Section 3.3 claiming the constraints are fully respected. Edge similarity and perceptual judgments cannot verify these properties; controlled rendered scenes with known scene parameters would provide substantially stronger validation.

Most quantitative evaluation uses model-generated sources with available generation trajectories, rather than arbitrary input images. This favors the setting in which source-feature reuse is easiest. The real-input experiment is valuable but compares only two baselines, omits commercial models and the underlying UniEdit-Flow editing pipeline, and does not clearly identify the backbone used in Table 12.

The claimed temporal-coherence advantage is not directly evaluated. Appendix A.5 averages image metrics over frames, and VIEScore independently assesses three sampled frames. These measurements do not establish reduced flicker, consistent color trajectories, or motion preservation.

The human-study protocol is internally inconsistent: Section B.2 describes pairwise comparisons, whereas Figure 22 asks participants to select one winner among nine methods. Table 7 reports preference shares summing to 100%, without explaining aggregation or the uncertainty terms. The reported 64.71% therefore cannot be interpreted confidently as a pairwise preference rate.

Novelty is primarily a targeted recombination of established attention-control ideas. The ablations do not quantitatively isolate the proposed quadrant choices against matched alternatives, and attribute reweighting lacks comparative or quantitative validation of controllability.

Important implementation and efficiency details remain unresolved. The paper does not clearly specify whether attention-block replacement occurs before or after softmax, how normalization is handled, or how attention masks are aggregated and normalized. Caching attention maps across layers and timesteps also has substantial potential storage and transfer costs; the claim of no additional computational cost is unsupported by runtime or memory measurements.

Superiority to commercial models is a preservation-versus-edit-success tradeoff rather than an unqualified improvement. Table 10 gives commercial models higher semantic-consistency scores, while ColorCtrl has higher perceptual quality and structural preservation. The paper's interpretation of stronger colors as unrealistic does not fully resolve whether requested edits were achieved.

strengths: ColorCtrl provides a useful, training-free adaptation of attention control to MM-DiT color editing. Combining visual attention transfer with masked value-token replacement produces convincing preservation of texture, geometry, and background.

Quantitative improvements are substantial and consistent across SD3, FLUX.1-dev, and CogVideoX on 40 PIE-Bench prompt pairs and 300 ColorCtrl-Bench pairs. On FLUX.1-dev, PIE-Bench Canny-SSIM reaches 0.9196 versus 0.8639 for the strongest competing training-free baseline, alongside improved background preservation and CLIP alignment.

The supplementary evaluation strengthens the evidence beyond CLIP: gradient-based metrics and VIEScore support improved structural preservation and editing quality. Table 12 also demonstrates gains on real-image editing, although with narrower comparisons.

Component ablations demonstrate complementary benefits from structure and color preservation. Qualitative results show promising multi-object editing, attribute-strength control, and compatibility with instruction-based editing models.
weaknesses: The claimed physical guarantees exceed the evidence. Transferring visual attention does not establish that geometry, materials, illumination intensity, or light transport remain fixed. Evaluation lacks controlled rendered scenes with ground-truth recoloring, and object-mask background metrics can penalize physically necessary changes in reflections or indirect illumination.

Most quantitative evaluation uses model-generated sources with cached generation trajectories and one fixed seed. This is useful for isolating editing behavior but favors the method's operating setting. Real-image evaluation includes only two baselines, omits the inversion provider UniEdit-Flow and commercial editors, and does not clearly identify the backbone used in Table 12.

The technical novelty is incremental relative to attention replacement and masked feature injection. Important implementation details remain unclear, including mask normalization and aggregation, and whether attention-quadrant replacement occurs before or after softmax. Post-softmax replacement can disrupt row normalization, whereas pre-softmax replacement does not preserve the original normalized visual attention.

Claims of superior temporal coherence are not directly tested: video metrics average frame-level scores rather than measuring flicker or motion consistency. Attribute re-weighting and instruction-model integration also lack quantitative evaluation or direct ablations against comparable controls.

The human-study protocol is inconsistent: Appendix B.2 describes pairwise comparisons, but Figure 22 shows selection of one winner among nine outputs, consistent with Table 7's preference shares summing to 100%. Case selection, aggregation, and the meaning of the reported uncertainty are unspecified. Commercial models also achieve higher semantic-consistency scores, so the evidence supports a preservation–edit-strength trade-off rather than unconditional superiority.

The claim of no additional computational cost excludes source-branch computation, attention-cache storage, and loading overhead. Runtime and peak-memory measurements are absent, particularly consequential for video attention. Code release is promised only upon acceptance.
